lesson.title: What is GDP?
lesson.summary: The most widely used indicator to measure the size of an economy — and its limitations.

blocks.text: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total value of all final goods and services produced in a country during a period, usually one year.
It is the main thermometer of a country's economic activity: it grows when the economy heats up and falls during recessions.
The most common formula is: GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + (Exports − Imports).
GDP measures everything, except that which makes life worthwhile. — Robert Kennedy

items: Does not measure inequality in income distribution
Can grow from harmful activities (pollution, wars)
Does not capture well-being or quality of life

cards.back: The total value of final goods and services produced in a country over a given period.

cards.front: What is the basic expenditure formula for GDP?
cards.back: GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + (Exports − Imports)

cards.front: Name two limitations of GDP as a measure of well-being.
cards.back: It does not measure inequality, ignores unpaid work, and can grow from harmful activities.

quiz.question: What type of production does GDP include?
options: All goods produced, including intermediate ones
Only final goods and services produced domestically
quiz.explanation: GDP counts only final goods and services to avoid double-counting intermediate inputs.

quiz.question: If a country's GDP rises due to a natural disaster that triggered reconstruction, this indicates:
options: That GDP can grow without reflecting an improvement in well-being
quiz.explanation: This is one of the main criticisms of GDP: economically costly activities can inflate it without generating real well-being.
